questions.q: List the six major supporting characters in "The Tiger King" and state one defining action or line for each.
questions.a: Correct answer: 1) Chief Astrologer — predicts death by the hundredth tiger; 2) Dewan — procures the hundredth tiger from Madras; 3) British Officer — wants to hunt tigers for photographs; 4) Duraisani — accepts all fifty diamond rings; 5) Hunters — kill the hundredth tiger secretly after the Maharaja misses; 6) Shopkeeper — sells a cheap wooden tiger for 300 rupees. A wrong answer (e.g., missing the duraisani or confusing the dewan with the astrologer) reveals the student cannot distinguish narrative functions: the astrologer sets the prophecy, the dewan executes the cover-up, the British officer represents colonial pressure, the duraisani embodies greed, the hunters represent systemic deceit, the shopkeeper represents exploitation.

questions.q: Explain how the dewan's character serves as a foil to the Maharaja. Use two textual details.
questions.a: Correct answer: The dewan is servile, pragmatic, and fearful where the Maharaja is arrogant, obsessive, and ruthless. When the Maharaja brandishes his gun, the dewan shudders and cries "I am not a tiger!" — highlighting the Maharaja's terror-inducing authority. Later, the dewan steals a tiger from People's Park to save his own job, showing moral flexibility the Maharaja lacks (the Maharaja at least hunts "honestly"). A wrong answer that calls the dewan "loyal" or "wise" misses the satire: the dewan's "loyalty" is self-preservation, and his "wisdom" is mere survival instinct. The foil exposes the Maharaja's tyranny by showing what it reduces subordinates to.

questions.q: The British officer never appears on stage — we only hear of him through the dewan and the Maharaja. Why does Kalki keep him offstage, and what does this achieve for the satire?
questions.a: Correct answer: Keeping the British officer offstage reduces him to a symbol of colonial entitlement — he wants only a photograph with a dead tiger, not the hunt itself. His absence makes his power more insidious: the Maharaja panics, bribes the duraisani with 3 lakh rupees, and risks his kingdom for a man who never speaks. This amplifies the satire on princely states' subservience to the British. A wrong answer focusing on "mystery" or "plot convenience" misses the political critique: the officer's invisibility mirrors how colonial authority operated through intermediaries, and the Maharaja's terror of an unseen man shows the hollowness of his "indomitable courage".

questions.q: Compare the hunters' cover-up of the missed shot with the shopkeeper's overpricing of the wooden tiger. What do these two episodes together reveal about the ecosystem of deceit around the Maharaja?
questions.a: Correct answer: Both episodes show how the Maharaja's absolute power corrupts everyone around him into complicity. The hunters kill the tiger secretly to save their jobs — "If he did, they could lose their jobs." The shopkeeper inflates the price 10,000-fold (2 annas → 300 rupees) fearing punishment under Emergency rules. Together they form a closed loop: the Maharaja's whim creates a reality where truth is dangerous and flattery is survival. A wrong answer treating them as isolated incidents misses the systemic point: the hunters' lie enables the Maharaja's false triumph; the shopkeeper's lie extracts wealth from that triumph. The wooden tiger's sliver — the instrument of the Maharaja's death — is purchased with money extorted by the same fear the hunters felt.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The chief astrologer is the only supporting character who speaks truth to power." Defend or refute with evidence.
questions.a: Correct answer: Refute. The astrologer's "truth" is a self-fulfilling prophecy wrapped in theatrical ambiguity. He says "death comes from the Tiger" but hedges: "Your majesty may kill ninety-nine tigers... But you must be very careful with the hundredth." He never challenges the Maharaja's killing spree; he only defines its terms. The real truth-tellers are the powerless: the dewan's wife (who helps drag the tiger), the hunters (who admit the miss to each other), the villagers (who report sheep disappearances). The astrologer serves the court; his prediction fuels the Maharaja's obsession. A wrong answer accepting the astrologer as a truth-teller confuses dramatic function with moral courage — he is the architect of the Maharaja's delusion, not its challenger.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the crown prince's perspective on the day he plays with the wooden tiger, revealing his understanding of his father's world.
questions.a: Expected answer: "Father laughed when the sliver pierced his hand. He didn't flinch — he never flinches, not at tigers, not at British officers, not at death. He thinks he's beaten the prophecy. The wooden tiger cost 300 rupees; the real ones cost him his kingdom. I'm three. I know better." A poor answer (e.g., "I played with my father. The tiger was rough. He got hurt.") reveals inability to adopt a perspective that synthesizes the story's irony — the child sees through the father's performance because he hasn't yet learned to fear it.
